main.t: The S-shaped collarbone at the front of the shoulder, joining the arm to the trunk (clavicle).

deeper.t: It is the only long bone in the body that lies horizontally.

facts.t: It lies at the front of the shoulder, so you can feel its whole length.
Its inner (medial) end joins the sternum. Its outer (lateral) end joins the acromion of the scapula.
With the scapula it forms the shoulder (pectoral) girdle.

simpler.t: It runs across the top of your chest, from your breastbone out to your shoulder.

deeper.t: Its joint with the sternum is the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.

items.name: Sternal end
items.t: The triangular inner end. It meets the manubrium of the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint.

items.name: Acromial end
items.t: The outer end. It meets the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint.

items.name: Shaft
items.t: The curved middle part between the two ends.

items.name: Underside of the acromial end
items.t: The strong coracoclavicular ligament anchors here, tying it to the coracoid process.

items.name: Near the sternal end
items.t: The costoclavicular ligament ties it to the first rib below.

simpler.t: It has an inner end, an outer end and a curved shaft between them.

deeper.t: The rough areas where muscles attach are more marked in manual workers.

facts.t: Anchored by muscles from above, it acts as a strut that holds the scapula out to the side.
This keeps the shoulder joint away from the trunk, giving the arm the widest range of movement.
It passes forces acting on the upper limb to the sternum and the axial skeleton.
It shields the nerves and blood vessels passing between the trunk and the upper limb.

simpler.t: The clavicle props your shoulder out to the side and passes force from your arm to your chest.

items.name: Sternoclavicular joint
items.t: A saddle joint with the manubrium. It lets the clavicle move up, down, forwards and back.

items.name: Acromioclavicular joint
items.t: A plane (gliding) joint with the acromion. Its own ligaments are fairly weak.

items.name: Coracoclavicular ligament
items.t: A very strong band to the coracoid process. It is the main support of the acromioclavicular joint.

items.name: Costoclavicular ligament
items.t: Ties the sternal end to the first rib and supports the sternoclavicular joint.

items.name: Articular disc
items.t: A pad of fibrocartilage inside the sternoclavicular joint unites the bones strongly.

items.name: Subclavian artery
items.t: Its name means “under the clavicle”. It becomes the axillary artery as it passes into the armpit.

items.name: Subclavian vein
items.t: The axillary vein becomes the subclavian vein as it passes into the thorax.

simpler.t: It joins the breastbone and the shoulder blade, and important vessels and nerves pass beneath it.

facts.t: It forms directly from membrane (intramembranous ossification), with no cartilage model: the only limb or girdle bone to do so.
The clavicle is the first bone in the body to start ossifying, in the fifth week of development.
Its ossification is not complete until about the age of 25.
In females, it tends to be shorter, thinner and less curved.
In males, it is heavier, longer and more curved, with rougher areas where muscles attach.

items.injury: A fall onto the outstretched arms, or a strong blow to the side of the shoulder.
items.damaged: The clavicle breaks, usually between its middle and outer parts. It is the bone broken most often.
items.cannotDo: Hold the arm up: the shoulder drops, and the patient supports the arm with the other hand.
items.why: The strong sternoclavicular joint rarely gives way, so the bone breaks. The weight of the arm then pulls the outer part down.

items.injury: A complete fracture of the clavicle.
items.damaged: The bone only, in most cases. The vessels and nerves beneath it are rarely hurt.
items.cannotDo: Move the shoulder without pain, though feeling and blood supply in the arm are usually normal.
items.why: Muscles across the shoulder pull the fragments forwards and inwards, away from the vessels and nerves.

items.q: Explain why a fall on the outstretched arm breaks the clavicle rather than dislocating the sternoclavicular joint.
model: The sternoclavicular joint is strong and rarely dislocated.
Force from the arm passes along the clavicle to the sternum.
The bone gives way first, usually between its middle and outer parts.
This makes the clavicle the bone broken most often.

items.q: Compare how the clavicle and the humerus develop.
model: Clavicle: directly from membrane (intramembranous ossification), with no cartilage model.
Humerus: a cartilage model replaced by bone (endochondral ossification).
The clavicle starts in the fifth week. The humerus has a primary centre in its shaft by the twelfth week.
The clavicle is not fully ossified until about 25.

items.q: Predict how a patient holds their arm after a complete fracture of the clavicle, and explain why.
model: The shoulder and outer fragment drop under the weight of the arm.
The patient supports the sagging arm with the other hand.
Muscles pull the outer fragment forwards and inwards.
So the two fragments override each other.

check.stem: Which is the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton?
check.why: The sternoclavicular joint, between the sternal end of the clavicle and the manubrium, is the only one.

options: From two halves that fuse at birth
check.why: It is the only limb or girdle bone that forms directly from membrane, without a cartilage model.

check.stem: Where does the clavicle usually break?
options: Between its middle and outer parts
check.why: Excess force usually breaks it between the middle and lateral parts of the bone.
